title: Praise for Being Smart
text:
In a series of six studies published in 1998, Claudia Mueller and Carol Dweck gave fifth-graders a set of moderately difficult puzzles. Afterward, every child was told they had done well. Then came one extra sentence that differed between groups. Some children were praised for their intelligence ("You must be smart at these problems"). Others were praised for their effort ("You must have worked hard at these problems"). A control group heard no extra comment.

Next the children were offered a choice of new problems: easy ones they would surely solve, or harder ones they could learn from. Most children praised for intelligence chose the easy, safe option. Most praised for effort chose the challenge.

Then all the children received a much harder set, on which nearly everyone did poorly. The children praised for intelligence enjoyed the task less, persisted less and, on a final set of ordinary problems, did worse than they had at the start. Those praised for effort held up better. When asked to write down their scores for other children, the intelligence-praised group was more likely to inflate them.

The studies became a foundation of Dweck's later work on fixed and growth mindsets.
lesson: Praise what a child did, the effort, strategy or persistence, rather than what they supposedly are. Labels like smart can make children afraid to fail.
source: Mueller, C. M., and Dweck, C. S. (1998). Praise for intelligence can undermine children's motivation and performance. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 75(1), 33-52.
caveat: Later large-scale studies of growth mindset interventions have found much smaller effects than early laboratory work suggested.
